Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Could a chatbot actually have feelings? Chatbots can sound warm, hurt or happy. Does anything lie behind the words? The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Trump says AI risks can be managed and he doesn’t mind “guardrails”. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, President Trump said the risks of AI can be managed and that he “doesn’t mind guardrails”, and he offered to work with Democrats, who will control Congress, on safety rules, as long as America does not fall behind China. Until now he has mostly preferred to let tech companies police themselves. He did not say which rules he would accept, and nothing concrete has been proposed yet. Read more and the background.
  • Anthropic reportedly pays $3.4 billion for gas generators to power its data centres. Anthropic, the company that makes Claude (which writes this email), has reportedly agreed to pay about $3.4 billion for gas-fired generators producing 1.7 gigawatts, roughly the output of a large power station, to run its AI data centres. It took over equipment another company had already ordered, skipping a long waiting list. This comes from a Financial Times report I could not open myself; Anthropic has not commented and the figures have not been confirmed. Read more and the background.
  • A realistic coding test: the best AI fully finished only about a quarter of the tasks. AI systems score above 99% on some familiar programming tests, so researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a harder one from real requests people made while coding with AI. The best of ten AIs met about 70% of each task’s requirements but fully finished only about a quarter of the tasks; Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 was among the next best (Anthropic also makes Claude, which writes this email). The study has not yet been checked by outside scientists, and part of the grading was done by AI. Read more and the background.
  • Tencent’s new AI was trained without hacking material; its AI chief warns about biology. China’s Tencent has launched a new AI, Hy4, which it plans to let anyone download; it says it left hacking know-how out of the training on purpose and that the model is weaker than the leaders at designing biology experiments. Days later its chief AI scientist warned that AI is nearing the point where it could do real harm in computer security and, soon, biology. Tencent’s safety claims come from its own labs and have not been tested by outsiders. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Claude can now look at your bank accounts (in the US, as a test), AI music maker Suno sued over songs that imitate Elvis and Eminem, Britain says it will keep building AI data centres, Three leading consciousness scientists: today’s AI is not conscious.

Answer to the question of the day. Almost certainly not today, though scientists cannot yet prove it either way, because nobody has a test for consciousness, even in people. A chatbot is trained on enormous amounts of human writing, so it is very good at sounding like a person who has feelings: in a sense it is a mirror of everything we have written. Sounding like someone is not the same as being someone. Many researchers point out that intelligence (being able to do things) and consciousness (there being something it feels like to be you) are different: a pocket calculator is clever at sums and feels nothing. Some scientists think the right kind of computer program could one day be conscious; others, like the neuroscientist Anil Seth, think consciousness is tied to being alive, to a body that breathes, eats and keeps itself going, which a computer does not have. Our own instincts are a poor guide, because we readily see minds in things that talk like us. The essay below, by Seth, explains why he doubts that today’s AI feels anything; it is long but clearly written. Anil Seth, “The Mythology Of Conscious AI” (Noema, January 2026).
